Future Perfect in Negative and Questions
We use the future perfect to talk about a future action that will finish before or around a certain time in the future.

The future tense is also used to talk about events that will last for a specified period of time at a determined moment in the future. Additionally, this tense is also used to express certainty regarding how completed an action is.

When we use the future perfect in negative we need to add not to will:

Subject + Will not (or won't) + Have+ Past participle

Example: By this time tomorrow, we won't have finished designing the website with CSS.

To form questions with this tense, add will before the subject:

Will+ Subject+ have+ past participle + ?

Example: Will you have set the styles for this web page by Monday?
This ensures that, by the time the website has been fully designed, pages won't have had different style throughout the site
Will programming have completely changed to CSS by the end of this decade?
Future Continuous in Negative and Questions
We use the future continuous to talk about an action that will be in progress at or around a time in the future.

We use the future continuous to predict a future action that will be in progress at or around some determined time in the future. This tense is also used to make guesses about the future.

If we want to use the future continuous in its negative form, we add not to will:

Subject + Will not (won't) + be + verb-ing

Example: You won't be using CSS for that website.

To make a question using this tense, we place will before the subject:

Will + Subject + Verb to be + Verb-ing + ?

Example: Will the designer be setting the website layout only with CSS?

images.text:
Edward: I don't understand why CSS was created in the first place.
Teacher: HTML was originally created to label web page content, but it was never designed to contain tags for formatting a website. That means tags like < font > had to be added to every single page when creating a large website. To tackle this issue, CSS was created. It has several benefits such as separation of the document content and its presentation. We'll be looking at some other benefits that will save us time and money. After these questions and answers, you won't be wasting your time creating a website the way you used to.

Edward: Ok, that helped me a lot, but what does CSS stand for?
Teacher: CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It sets the styles in a website, which include the color, font, and layout in a different file. CSS also describes how the HTML elements will be presented on screen, paper or other media.
Edward: Wait! Will I be using a style sheet that doesn't allow me to modify the style?
Teacher: No! The style definition is usually stored in .css files, which can be modified from the outside. This ensures that, by the time the website has been fully designed, pages won't have had different style throughout the site. Also, you can modify the entire look of a website by just changing one file!

Edward: But, does it work in any browser? If I need to create a website, will I be using CSS?
Teacher: Support for CSS is not fully compatible with all web browsers. However, there are some CSS hacks that work as a clean coding technique, thus the search engine won't have difficulties reading your website content. This will ensure that when you've finished your website, visitors won't be looking at any other websites but yours. In addition, it makes your website available in different viewing formats.
Many programmers who have already created a website using tables might be reluctant to change to CSS as it will take some time. Nevertheless, the benefits outweigh the effort. With more and more web designers changing to this, we must ask ourselves: will programming have completely changed to CSS by the end of this decade?
